mainTopic: Rain in the פסוקים and in prayer: rain compared to birth, praying in times of trouble, and the blessing of rain
overview: The גמרא finishes comparing rain to a woman having a child, using three shared words: closing up, giving birth, and remembering. It explains 'פלג אלהים' as a dome in the sky that rain comes out of. רבי שמואל בר נחמני explains a פסוק in איוב about rain that comes as punishment or as kindness. Then come two stories about times of trouble. In a famine and plague, רבי שמואל בר נחמני said to pray about the famine, because food is given only to the living. Under a decree that banned fasting, רבי זירא told the people to accept a fast and keep it later. Next, רבי יצחק and others teach about rain: it can be a burden at the wrong time but a great blessing in its time, and blessing rests only on what is hidden from the eye. The amud ends with a series of רבי יוחנן's teachings on the greatness of rain, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Closing up is said about both a woman and rain
steps.stepSummary: The same word, עצירה (closing up), is used for a woman who cannot have children and for the sky holding back rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'closing up' is used about a woman, as it says: 'For ה׳ had fast closed up every womb.' And the word 'closing up' is used about rain, as it says: 'And He will close up the heavens.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the first of three word-links between a woman and rain: both can be 'closed up.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman who cannot have children is described with the word עצר. The sky not giving rain is described with the same word. This shared word is the first sign that the תורה treats rain like birth.

keyTerms.meaning: It was said (the word is used in a פסוק)

phrases.english: Closing up is said about a woman,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״כִּי עָצֹר עָצַר ה׳ בְּעַד כׇּל רֶחֶם״,
phrases.english: as it says: 'For ה׳ had fast closed up every womb,'
and closing up is said about rain,
as it is written: 'And He will close up the heavens.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the comparison of rain to birth from just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word עצירה links a woman who cannot have children with a sky that holds back rain.

steps.title: Giving birth is said about both a woman and rain
steps.stepSummary: The word לידה (giving birth) is used for a woman and for rain making the earth produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'giving birth' is used about a woman, and also about rain. About a woman: 'And she conceived and gave birth to a son.' About rain: 'And it makes the earth give birth and sprout.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second word-link: both a woman and rain are connected to 'giving birth.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: First the גמרא states the parallel in general, then brings a פסוק for each side. Rain makes the earth 'give birth' to plants, just like a mother gives birth to a child.

keyTerms.meaning: And it makes it give birth

phrases.english: Giving birth is said about a woman
and giving birth is said about rain.
Giving birth is said about a woman,
as it is written: 'And she conceived and gave birth to a son,'
and giving birth is said about rain,
as it is written: 'And it makes it give birth and sprout.'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 55:10. The rain is what makes the earth 'give birth.'

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר לֵידָה בְּאִשָּׁה וְנֶאֱמַר לֵידָה בִּגְשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second word-link in the same pattern as step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word לידה links a woman giving birth with rain making the earth produce.

steps.title: Remembering is said about both a woman and rain
steps.stepSummary: The word פקידה (remembering) is used for ה׳ remembering שרה and for ה׳ remembering the land with rain.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'remembering' is used about a woman, and also about rain. About a woman: 'And ה׳ remembered שרה.' About rain: 'You remembered the land and watered it, greatly enriching it; the stream of God is full of water.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third and last word-link: ה׳ 'remembers' both a woman and the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When ה׳ 'remembered' שרה, she had a child. When ה׳ 'remembers' the land, He waters it with rain. The same word shows that rain is like the gift of a child.
steps.whatToRemember: Three words connect a woman and rain: עצירה (closing up), לידה (giving birth), and פקידה (remembering). The point is that rain is like the birth of a child.

phrases.english: Remembering is said about a woman,
and remembering is said about rain.
Remembering is said about a woman,
as it is written: 'And ה׳ remembered שרה,'
and remembering is said about rain,
as it is written: 'You remembered the land and watered it,'
greatly enriching it;
the stream of God is full of water.'

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶאֱמַר פְּקִידָה בְּאִשָּׁה, וְנֶאֱמַר פְּקִידָה בִּגְשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the set of three word-links.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word פקידה links ה׳ remembering a barren woman with ה׳ sending rain to the land.

steps.title: What does 'the stream of God full of water' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the phrase 'פלג אלהים מלא מים' from the last פסוק means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'the stream of God is full of water'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the comparison to ask about a puzzling phrase in the פסוק it just quoted. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack; it is a request for an explanation. The question is what 'God's stream' up above, full of water, actually is.

phrases.english: What is 'the stream of God is full of water'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up a phrase from the פסוק quoted in step 3 and asks for its meaning.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of 'פלג אלהים מלא מים'.

steps.title: A dome in the sky that rain comes out of
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that there is a kind of dome in the sky, and rain comes out of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: There is something like a dome in the sky, and rain comes out from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by quoting a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'stream of God full of water' is a dome-like store in the sky. Rain comes down from it to the earth.

phrases.english: It was taught: There is something like a dome in the sky,
from which rain comes out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'פלג אלהים' is a dome-like store in the sky that rain comes out of.

steps.title: Rain as punishment or kindness: where it falls
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני explains a פסוק in איוב: when people deserve punishment, rain falls on mountains and hills, and when they deserve kindness, it falls on fields and vineyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said: What does the פסוק mean, 'Whether for punishment, or for His land, or for kindness He brings it'? 'For punishment' means the rain falls on mountains and hills. 'For kindness He brings it to His land' means it falls on fields and vineyards.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues talking about rain and brings a new teaching from רבי שמואל בר נחמני on a פסוק in איוב. He explains that the same rain can be a punishment or a blessing, depending on where it lands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rain on mountains and hills mostly runs off and helps very few people, so it counts as a punishment. Rain on fields and vineyards feeds the crops people live on, so it is a kindness. He reads 'for His land' together with 'for kindness,' so the פסוק really describes two cases, not three.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'a rod'; here it means punishment
Mountains and hills, places where rain does little good
Fields and vineyards, places where rain helps people most

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said:
What is the meaning of what is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״אִם לְשֵׁבֶט אִם לְאַרְצוֹ אִם לְחֶסֶד יַמְצִאֵהוּ״.
phrases.english: "Whether for punishment, or for His land, or for kindness He brings it"?
"Whether for punishment": on mountains and on hills;
"If for kindness, He brings it to His land":
phrases.notes: He moves 'for His land' next to 'for kindness,' so the two phrases are read as one idea.

phrases.english: on fields and on vineyards.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of rain with a new explanation of a פסוק by a new speaker.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain that falls on mountains and hills is a punishment; rain that falls on fields and vineyards is a kindness.

steps.title: A second reading: trees, seeds, and water storage
steps.stepSummary: A second explanation of the same פסוק: the three phrases match three levels of rain, one good only for trees, one good for seeds, and one that fills water pits and caves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another explanation: 'For punishment' means rain good only for trees. 'For His land' means rain good for seeds. 'For kindness He brings it' means rain that fills cisterns, ditches, and caves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to read the same פסוק. This time each of the three phrases stands for its own kind of rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first reading, the פסוק had two parts. Here it has three levels, from least helpful to most helpful. The best rain, called 'kindness,' fills the water pits with enough water to last through the dry season.

keyTerms.meaning: Cisterns, ditches, and caves: places that store water

phrases.english: "Whether for punishment": for trees;
phrases.notes: Here the punishment is rain that helps only the trees.

phrases.english: "Or for His land": for seeds;
"Or for kindness He brings it":
cisterns, ditches, and caves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different explanation of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three phrases match three levels of rain: rain only for trees, rain for seeds, and rain that fills the water stores.

steps.title: Famine and plague: what should the people pray for?
steps.stepSummary: In the days of רבי שמואל בר נחמני there was both a famine and a plague. The חכמים believed they could not pray about both, so they decided to pray about the plague and put up with the famine.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the days of רבי שמואל בר נחמני there was a famine and a plague. They said: What should we do? Should we pray for mercy about both? That is not possible. Instead, let us pray about the plague, and we will put up with the famine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about two troubles that came at the same time. This step sets up the problem, and the next step gives רבי שמואל בר נחמני's advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים take for granted a rule that you do not pray about two troubles at once. Since they had to pick one, they chose the plague and agreed to put up with the famine. The source for this rule comes a few steps later.

keyTerms.meaning: We will put up with it

phrases.english: In the days of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
there was a famine and a plague.
They said: What should we do?
Should we pray for mercy about both?
That is not possible.
Rather, let us pray for mercy about the plague,
and the famine we will put up with.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּימֵי רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי הֲוָה כַּפְנָא וּמוֹתָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining פסוקים to a story from the time of the same חכם.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: With two troubles and only one allowed prayer, which one should they pray about?

steps.title: Pray about the famine, because plenty is given to the living
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני tells them to pray about the famine, because when ה׳ sends plenty He gives it to living people, so the plague will stop as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said to them: Let us pray about the famine. When the Merciful One gives plenty, He gives it to the living, as it says: 'You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני disagrees with the חכמים' plan and tells them to pray about the famine instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ satisfies 'every living thing.' So if ה׳ answers the prayer for food, He has to send it to people who are alive, which means the plague will end too. Praying about the famine actually takes care of both troubles.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, a name for ה׳

steps.whatToRemember: By praying for one thing, plenty of food, which can only go to the living, you also get the second thing, an end to the plague.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said to them:
Let us pray for mercy about the famine,
because when the Merciful One gives plenty,
it is to the living that He gives it,
phrases.notes: So He will have to stop the plague too, so there are living people to eat the food.

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״פּוֹתֵחַ אֶת יָדֶךָ וּמַשְׂבִּיעַ לְכׇל חַי רָצוֹן״.
phrases.english: as it is written: "You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing with favor."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי: נִיבְעֵי רַחֲמֵי אַכַּפְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the חכמים' question and changes their plan.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Pray about the famine, because plenty from ה׳ goes to the living, so the plague will end as well.

steps.title: Where do we learn not to pray about two troubles?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the rule, used in the story, that we do not pray about two troubles at once.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that we do not pray about two troubles at once?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask where the rule in the story comes from. This sets up the proofs in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים in the story simply took the rule for granted. Now the גמרא wants a source in a פסוק for it.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that we do not pray about two troubles at once?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule assumed in the story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in a פסוק for not praying about two troubles at once.

steps.title: Proof from עזרא: 'for this'
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק in עזרא says they fasted and prayed 'for this,' which shows there was another trouble they did not pray about.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'So we fasted and asked our G-d for this.' This shows there was another trouble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק from עזרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'for this' point to one specific trouble. That means another trouble was going on at the same time, and they chose not to pray about it. That is the source for praying about only one trouble at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: For this, about this one thing
Which shows, from this we learn

phrases.english: As it is written: "So we fasted and asked our God for this."
This shows that there was another trouble.
phrases.notes: 'For this' means only this one, so another trouble was left out of the prayer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'this' in the פסוק in עזרא shows they prayed about one trouble even though there was another.

steps.title: Proof from דניאל, as taught in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: In ארץ ישראל they learned the same rule, in the name of רבי חגי, from a פסוק in דניאל: they asked for mercy 'about this secret,' which shows there was another trouble.
steps.simpleTranslation: In ארץ ישראל they say, in the name of רבי חגי, that we learn it from here: 'To ask for mercy from the G-d of heaven about this secret.' This shows there was another trouble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second source for the same rule, from the חכמים of ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This proof works the same way as the one from עזרא. The word 'this' in 'this secret' shows they prayed about only one matter while another was also going on. The only difference is which פסוק is used.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: We do not pray about two troubles at the same time. Both proofs come from the word 'this' in a פסוק, which shows that only one trouble was prayed about.

phrases.aramaic: בְּמַעְרְבָא אָמְרִי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חַגַּי מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: In the West they say in the name of Rabbi Chaggai: it is learned from here:
phrases.notes: 'The West' is ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

phrases.aramaic: ״וְרַחֲמִין לְמִבְעֵא מִן קֳדָם אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא עַל רָזָא דְּנָה״,
phrases.english: "And to ask for mercy from before the God of heaven about this secret."
This shows that there was another trouble.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמַעְרְבָא אָמְרִי מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חַגַּי מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different פסוק as the source for the same rule.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we do not pray about two troubles at once.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דניאל 2:18: 'about this secret,' which shows there was another matter they did not pray about.

steps.title: רבי זירא tells the people to accept a fast they cannot yet keep
steps.stepSummary: In the days of רבי זירא the government passed a decree of persecution that banned fasting. רבי זירא told the people to accept a fast now and keep it once the decree was cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the days of רבי זירא, a decree of persecution was passed, and it was decreed that people may not fast. רבי זירא said to them: Let us accept the fast upon ourselves, and when the persecution is cancelled, we will keep it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells another story about a time of trouble. This time the people could not even fast, so רבי זירא found a way around it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the response to a decree is a fast. Here the decree itself banned fasting. רבי זירא's idea is that simply accepting the fast already counts, even though the actual fasting comes later.

keyTerms.meaning: To observe a fast (literally, to 'sit' in a fast)
Let us accept it upon ourselves

phrases.english: In the days of Rabbi Zeira
they decreed a persecution
and they decreed not to sit in a fast
phrases.notes: 'Sit in a fast' just means to keep a fast day.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said to them
Let us accept it upon ourselves
and when the persecution is cancelled, we will keep it

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about how to respond to a time of trouble, following the story of רבי שמואל בר נחמני.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under a decree that bans fasting, one may accept a fast now and keep it once the decree is cancelled.

steps.title: The people ask רבי זירא for his source
steps.stepSummary: The people ask רבי זירא how he knows that accepting a fast without keeping it yet has any value.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: From where do you have this?
steps.whatsHappening: The people ask for a source for רבי זירא's idea. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether just accepting a fast, without actually fasting, accomplishes anything. They want a פסוק that shows it does.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you know this?

phrases.english: They said to him
From where do you have this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבי זירא's ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that accepting a fast before keeping it is effective.

steps.title: רבי זירא brings a proof from דניאל
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא quotes the פסוק where the angel tells דניאל that his words were heard from the first day he set his heart to fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: As it is written, 'And he said to me: Do not fear, דניאל, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to fast before your God, your words were heard.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers with a פסוק from דניאל. It shows that prayer is accepted from the moment a person decides to fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'from the first day that you set your heart,' not from the day you finished fasting. So the decision itself is what counts, and that is why accepting the fast now has value.
steps.whatToRemember: A decision to fast already counts, so one may accept a fast now even if the actual fasting must wait.

phrases.english: He said to them: As it is written
"And he said to me: Do not fear, Daniel
for from the first day
that you set your heart
to understand and to fast before your God
your words were heard"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק in דניאל shows prayer is heard from the moment one sets his heart to fast.

steps.title: Rain on Friday is a sign of a curse, even in a drought
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that even in years of terrible drought like the days of אליהו, rain that falls on ערב שבת is only a sign of a curse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: Even in years like the years of אליהו, if rain falls on Fridays, it is nothing but a sign of a curse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to talking about rain. רבי יצחק says rain on ערב שבת is a bad sign, even when people badly need rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You would think any rain in a drought is a blessing. רבי יצחק says that rain at the wrong time, on ערב שבת, is still a curse. The text does not give the reason here.

keyTerms.meaning: The years of אליהו, when no rain fell

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak said
Even in years like the years of Eliyahu
phrases.notes: Those were the years when אליהו stopped the rain, so people were desperate for it.

phrases.english: if rain fell on Fridays
it is nothing but a sign of a curse

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אֲפִילּוּ שָׁנִים כִּשְׁנֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of fasting and returns to statements about rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain on ערב שבת is a sign of a curse, even in a drought.

steps.title: רבה בר שילא: a rainy day is as hard as a day of judgment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא connects רבי יצחק's teaching to the words of רבה בר שילא, who said a rainy day is as hard as a day of judgment.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רבה בר שילא said: A day of rain is as hard as a day of judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that another אמורא said something similar. This backs up the idea that rain can be a burden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'הַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר' mean 'this matches what someone else said.' The גמרא is telling us that רבה בר שילא's saying, that a rainy day is as hard as a day of judgment, expresses the same idea as רבי יצחק's teaching.

phrases.english: This is what Rabba bar Sheila said
A day of rain is hard
like a day of judgment

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 16 by matching it to another statement.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יצחק's teaching that rain can be a curse.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה בר שילא's statement that a rainy day is as hard as a day of judgment.

steps.title: אמימר: if people did not need rain, we would pray to stop it
steps.stepSummary: אמימר says that if rain were not needed by people, we would pray for mercy to cancel it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר said: If not for the fact that people need it, we would ask for mercy and cancel it.
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר adds another statement about how bothersome rain is. He says the only reason we do not pray against it is that we need it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes even further than step 17. Rain is such a bother that we would pray to stop it completely, but people's need for it outweighs that.

phrases.english: Ameimar said
If not for the fact that people need it
we would ask for mercy and cancel it

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַמֵּימָר: אִי לָא דִּצְרִיךְ לִבְרִיָּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a stronger statement about how bothersome rain is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is so bothersome that we would pray against it if people did not need it.

steps.title: Sun on שבת is charity for the poor
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that sunshine on שבת is charity for the poor, and brings a פסוק from מלאכי about a 'sun of charity.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: Sun on שבת is charity for the poor, as it says: 'And there will shine for you who fear My name a sun of charity and healing.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק gives another teaching about weather on שבת. Sunshine on שבת is a kindness to poor people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the opposite of rain on ערב שבת. The proof is the פסוק's words 'שֶׁמֶשׁ צְדָקָה,' a sun of charity.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said
Sun on Shabbat
is charity for the poor
as it says: "And there will shine for you who fear My name
a sun of charity and healing"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching of רבי יצחק about weather around שבת, the opposite case of step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sunshine on שבת is charity for the poor.

steps.title: A day of rain is great: even a coin in the pocket is blessed
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that a day of rain is so great that even a פרוטה in one's pocket is blessed, based on a פסוק in דברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יצחק said: Great is the day of rains, for even a פרוטה in the pocket is blessed on it, as it says: 'To give the rain of your land in its time, and to bless all the work of your hand.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק now turns to praising rain. On a day of rain, blessing reaches even money that has nothing to do with farming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק puts rain together with blessing 'all the work of your hand.' So the blessing of rain spreads beyond crops, even to a coin in a pocket. This balances the earlier steps that spoke about how hard a rainy day can be.

keyTerms.meaning: Great is the day of rains
A small coin in the pocket

steps.whatToRemember: Rain at the wrong time can be a curse and a burden, but rain in its proper time brings blessing to everything, even a coin in your pocket.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said
Great is the day of rains
for even a perutah in the pocket
is blessed on it
as it says: "To give the rain of your land in its time
and to bless all the work of your hand"

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching of רבי יצחק, this time praising rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A day of rain brings blessing even to a coin in one's pocket.

steps.title: Blessing rests only on what is hidden from the eye
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק teaches that blessing is found only in things hidden from view, based on a פסוק about storehouses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said: Blessing is found only in something hidden from the eye, as the פסוק says: 'ה׳ will command the blessing with you in your storehouses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רבי יצחק about blessing. He says blessing only rests on things that are hidden and not seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word באסמיך (your storehouses) sounds like סמוי (hidden). רבי יצחק reads the פסוק as saying that blessing goes to things stored away out of sight. This follows naturally from the previous step, where he taught that a פרוטה in one's pocket is blessed on a day of rain.

keyTerms.meaning: Hidden from the eye, out of sight

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Blessing is not found
except in something hidden from the eye,
as it says:
"ה׳ will command the blessing with you
in your storehouses."
phrases.notes: דברים 28:8. The word אסמיך sounds like סמוי, "hidden." That is the link.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another teaching of רבי יצחק on blessing, extending the idea of the blessed פרוטה in the pocket from step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blessing rests only on things hidden from view, learned from באסמיך / סמוי.

steps.title: The school of רבי ישמעאל teaches the same idea
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל teaches the same principle, using the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: Blessing is found only in something the eye does not control, as the פסוק says: 'ה׳ will command the blessing with you in your storehouses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching from the school of רבי ישמעאל that says the same thing as רבי יצחק. This backs up his idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording is slightly different, 'something the eye does not control,' but the point is the same. Blessing does not come to things that are on display. Because a תנא from a ברייתא says it, רבי יצחק's teaching now has older support.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching taught in the study hall of רבי ישמעאל

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Blessing is not found

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין הָעַיִן שׁוֹלֶטֶת בּוֹ,
phrases.english: except in something the eye does not control,
phrases.notes: He means something that people's eyes cannot see or look over.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״יְצַו ה׳ אִתְּךָ אֶת הַבְּרָכָה בַּאֲסָמֶיךָ״.
phrases.english: as it says: "ה׳ will command the blessing with you in your storehouses."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יצחק's teaching with a parallel ברייתא that uses the same פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יצחק's principle that blessing rests only on hidden things
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל, using דברים 28:8

steps.title: How to pray for blessing when measuring grain
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches what a farmer says before and during measuring his grain, and that praying after measuring is a vain prayer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: One who goes in to measure his grain pile says: 'May it be Your will, ה׳ our God, that You send blessing in the work of our hands.' Once he starts measuring, he says: 'Blessed is the One Who sends blessing in this pile.' If he measured first and then prayed, that is a vain prayer, because blessing is not found in something weighed, measured, or counted, only in something hidden from the eye.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that puts the principle into practice. A farmer must pray for blessing on his grain before he measures it, not after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before measuring, the amount is still unknown, so it is 'hidden,' and blessing can still rest on it. Once the grain is measured, its amount is known, and asking for more would mean asking for an open miracle. That is why such a prayer is called a vain prayer.

keyTerms.meaning: Threshing floor; the farmer's grain pile
A heap or pile of grain

steps.whatToRemember: Blessing rests on what is still unknown and hidden. Once something is weighed, measured, or counted, it is too late to pray for more.
steps.confusionAlert: Here בְּרָכָה means 'blessing' in the sense of abundance, but the verb בֵּירַךְ ('he blessed') refers to the farmer saying his prayer. Do not mix up the two.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who goes in to measure his grain pile says:
"May it be Your will, ה׳ our God,
that You send blessing in the work of our hands."
Once he began to measure, he says:
"Blessed is the One Who sends blessing in this pile."
If he measured and only afterward prayed for blessing —
that is a vain prayer,
because blessing is not found

phrases.aramaic: לֹא בְּדָבָר הַשָּׁקוּל, וְלֹא בְּדָבָר הַמָּדוּד,
phrases.english: not in something weighed, and not in something measured,
and not in something counted,
but only in something hidden from the eye.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הַנִּכְנָס לָמוֹד אֶת גׇּרְנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the principle 'blessing rests only on hidden things' to a practical case and spells out its halachic result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pray for blessing before and while measuring. A prayer said after measuring is a תפלת שוא.
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns an אגדה idea into a practical rule about when a prayer for blessing makes sense.

steps.title: A day of rain is as great as the gathering of the exiles
steps.stepSummary: After a memory aid for רבי יוחנן's teachings, he teaches that a rainy day is as great as קיבוץ גליות, based on the word אפיקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Memory aid: Gathering, armies, charity, tithe, provider. רבי יוחנן said: A day of rain is as great as the day of the gathering of the exiles, as it says: 'Return our captivity, ה׳, like streams in the dry land.' And 'streams' means rain, as it says: 'And the streams of the sea appeared.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא first gives a memory aid listing a series of רבי יוחנן's teachings. Then it begins with the first one: a rainy day is as great as קיבוץ גליות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the return of the exiles is compared to אפיקים in the dry south. A second פסוק shows that אפיקים refers to rain. So rain is placed side by side with the great day of redemption.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid that lists the coming teachings
The gathering of the exiles back to ארץ ישראל
Streams or water channels, here understood as rain

phrases.aramaic: קִבּוּץ, גְּיָיסוֹת, צְדָקָה, מַעֲשֵׂר, פַּרְנָס סִימָן.
phrases.english: Gathering, armies, charity, tithe, provider: this is a memory aid.
phrases.notes: Each word hints at one of רבי יוחנן's coming teachings. The first three come here, the fourth starts at the very end of this amud, and the rest continue on the next amud.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
A day of rain is as great
as the day of the gathering of the exiles,
as it says:
"Return our captivity, ה׳,
like streams in the dry land,"
and "streams" means nothing other than rain,
as it says: "And the streams of the sea appeared."

steps.triggerLanguage: קִבּוּץ, גְּיָיסוֹת, צְדָקָה, מַעֲשֵׂר, פַּרְנָס סִימָן. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the theme of the greatness of rain (steps 16-20) with a new series of teachings by רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A day of rain is as great as קיבוץ גליות, because the פסוק compares the return of the exiles to אפיקים, which means rain.

steps.title: Even armies stop fighting on a rainy day
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that rain is so great that even troops halt on that day, reading גדודיה as 'its troops.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: A day of rain is great, for even armies stop on it, as it says: 'Watering its ridges abundantly, settling its furrows.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is רבי יוחנן's second teaching, the 'armies' from the memory aid. On a day of rain, even armies stop fighting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word גדודיה in the פסוק means furrows, but גדודים can also mean troops. רבי יוחנן reads it both ways: the rain 'settles down' the troops, so fighting stops.

keyTerms.meaning: Its furrows; also hints at 'its troops'

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
A day of rain is great,
for even armies stop on it,
as it says:
"Watering its ridges abundantly,
settling its furrows."
phrases.notes: תהלים 65:11. The word גדודים can mean furrows or troops, so it hints that the troops settle down.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: גָּדוֹל יוֹם הַגְּשָׁמִים, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ גְּיָיסוֹת פּוֹסְקוֹת בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second teaching in רבי יוחנן's series, matching 'גייסות' in the memory aid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is so great that even armies stop fighting on a rainy day, read from גדודיה.

steps.title: Rain is held back because of people who pledge charity and do not give
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that rain is withheld because of people who publicly pledge צדקה but do not pay, based on a פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Rain is held back only because of those who pledge צדקה in public and do not give, as it says: 'Clouds and wind, but no rain: a man who boasts of a false gift.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is רבי יוחנן's third teaching, the 'charity' from the memory aid. He names one cause of drought: empty public pledges of צדקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק compares someone who brags about a gift he never gives to clouds and wind that bring no rain. רבי יוחנן reads this as cause and effect: empty promises lead to empty skies. The punishment matches the sin, since a promise without giving brings clouds without rain.

keyTerms.meaning: People who pledge (set an amount for) charity

steps.whyThisMatters: It ties the theme of rain back to how a person behaves. Keeping one's public promises of צדקה is connected to receiving rain.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Rain is not held back
except because of those who pledge charity in public
and do not give,
as it says:
"Clouds and wind, but no rain:
a man who boasts of a false gift."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֵין הַגְּשָׁמִים נֶעֱצָרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third teaching in רבי יוחנן's series, matching 'צדקה' in the memory aid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain is withheld because of those who publicly pledge צדקה and do not give it.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן opens another teaching on a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces one more teaching from רבי יוחנן, using the opening formula 'What is the meaning of that which is written.' The פסוק and his explanation follow next.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: What is the meaning of that which is written?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is preparing to quote a פסוק and give רבי יוחנן's explanation of it, which comes in the very next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'And' links this teaching to the chain of רבי יוחנן teachings in steps 24-26. The question 'מאי דכתיב' is not a challenge. It is a standard way of saying 'Let me explain this פסוק.' No new idea has been taught yet. That happens once the פסוק is quoted.

keyTerms.meaning: And he said. It adds another teaching from the same speaker.
The אמורא whose string of teachings the גמרא is collecting here
What is the meaning of what is written? This is a formula for opening an explanation of a פסוק.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'מאי דכתיב' as a question attacking the פסוק. It just announces that a פסוק is about to be explained.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
What is the meaning of that which is written:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of רבי יוחנן's teachings after his statement about pledging צדקה publicly and not paying it (step 26).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line introduces a פסוק that רבי יוחנן will explain next.
